The 'Equivalent definition (Garnett (5.1))' inside the Nevanlinna-class definition is proved there, so it is a nested claim (proved by its proof) rather than part of the definition.

Almost all results are Garnett's theorems restated for formalization, marked external per Hard rule 3 although the blueprint re-proves them; uncited classical facts (Poisson formula, Harnack, Lebesgue differentiation) are external standard; only Lean-specific lemmas are origin paper.
Proofs refer to Garnett's own numbering in words ('(5.1)', '(5.9)', 'II.4.1', '(5.2) and (5.3)') rather than \ref; these were mapped to the blueprint nodes stating them by hand, with basis named.

nodes.name: Poisson integral of boundary data
nodes.statement:
Boundary data is a vector measure $
u$ with values in a real normed space, and \[ P[
u](w)=\int P_w(z)\,d
u(z). \] The kernel is real-valued, so it pairs with $
u$ by scalar multiplication. A finite positive measure $\mu$ enters as the associated signed measure, and data given as a function $f$ against a reference measure $\mu$ enters as the vector measure $f\,d\mu$. For a finite positive measure, compatibility with the ordinary integral gives $P[\mu](w)=\int P_w\,d\mu$ for every $w$, without a support hypothesis. This follows from the integral pairing identity for the associated signed measure.

For vector measures, $P[-

u$ carried by the same circle, $P_w$ is integrable against $|
u|$ and its Jordan decomposition gives \[ P[
u](w)=\int P_w\,d
u^+-\int P_w\,d
u^-. \] Differences of finite positive measures carried by the circle are still carried by the circle, and their Poisson integrals subtract accordingly. At an interior point the kernel is bounded on the boundary circle, which gives the stated integrability. Split a real density into its positive and negative parts to obtain the density formula. nodes.name: Poisson integrals of boundary data are harmonic
nodes.statement: For a finite positive measure $\mu$ carried by the circle and real $k\in L^1(\mu)$, both $P[\mu]$ and $P[k\,d\mu]$ are harmonic inside. If $f$ is continuous on $\partial\D(c,R)$ then $P[f\,d\sigma]$ is harmonic on the open disc, where $\sigma$ is normalized arclength. \begin{proof} For a positive measure, take the real part of its analytic Herglotz--Riesz transform. For a real density, split it into its positive and negative parts and use linearity. Harmonicity of the circle average follows from harmonicity of the kernel in the interior variable, by differentiating under the integral sign. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Nontangential approach region
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.4}{Chapter I, Section 4, printed page 21, PDF page 33, disc form} For $\zeta\in\partial\D$ and $\alpha>1$ put \[ \Gamma_\alpha(\zeta) =\Bigl\{z\in\D:\ |\zeta-z|<\alpha\,(1-|z|)\Bigr\}, \] a teardrop-shaped region asymptotic at $\zeta$ to an angle with vertex $\zeta$. Facts to record: $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$ is open and contained in $\D$; it increases with $\alpha$; it contains the radial segment $[0,1)\zeta$; it is empty when $\alpha\le 1$; and $\Gamma_\alpha(1)$ is mathlib's \texttt{Complex.stolzSet}~$\alpha$, with $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)=\zeta\cdot\Gamma_\alpha(1)$. Mathlib only has the region at $\zeta=1$, so the rotated family has to be added.

nodes.name: Nontangential limit
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.5}{Chapter I, Section 5, printed page 27, PDF page 39} Write $\mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta)$ for the neighbourhood filter of $\zeta$ within $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$. The \emph{nontangential filter} at $\zeta$ is their supremum in the lattice of filters, \[ \mathcal{N}_\zeta=\sup_{\alpha>1}\ \mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta). \] For $\alpha>1$, $f$ has limit $L$ at $\zeta$ \emph{within} $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$ if $f\to L$ along $\mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta)$, and $f$ has \emph{nontangential limit} $L$ at $\zeta$ if $f\to L$ along $\mathcal{N}_\zeta$. The two are related by \[ f\to L \ \text{along}\ \mathcal{N}_\zeta \iff \forall\,\alpha>1,\ f\to L \ \text{along}\ \mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta). \]

nodes.label: def:nt_limit

nodes.name: Boundary value
nodes.statement: The boundary value of $f$ at $\zeta$ is \[ f^*(\zeta)=\lim_{\mathcal{N}_\zeta}f, \] the limit along the nontangential filter $\mathcal{N}_\zeta$, read through the choice operator so that it is a total function. Where the nontangential limit at $\zeta$ exists, it equals $f^*(\zeta)$.

nodes.statement_short: $f^*(\zeta)$ is the (choice-operator) limit of $f$ along the nontangential filter.
nodes.genus: the limit along the nontangential filter $\mathcal{N}_\zeta$

nodes.name: The nontangential filter is nontrivial
nodes.statement: For $\zeta\in\partial\D$ and $\alpha>1$ the radial segment $[0,1)\zeta$ lies in $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$; hence $\mathcal{N}_\zeta\neq\bot$. \begin{proof} For $0\le r<1$ one has $|r\zeta|=r<1$ and $|\zeta-r\zeta|=1-r<\alpha(1-r)$. So $\zeta$ lies in the closure of $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$, making $\mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta)$ nontrivial; a supremum of filters is nontrivial as soon as one of them is, so a single $\alpha$ suffices. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Poisson kernel over a Stolz region
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha>1$. There is a constant $C_\alpha$ such that for every $\zeta\in\partial\D$, every $z\in\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$ and every $\theta$, \[ P_z(\theta)\ \le\ \frac{C_\alpha\,(1-|z|)}{\bigl((1-|z|)+|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|\bigr)^{2}} . \] In particular $P_z(\theta)\le C_\alpha/(1-|z|)$ always, and $P_z(\theta)\le C_\alpha (1-|z|)/|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|^{2}$ once $|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|\ge 2\alpha(1-|z|)$. Together with $\int P_z\,d\theta/2\pi=1$ this exhibits the Poisson kernels, restricted to a Stolz region, as an approximate identity with a uniformly integrable decreasing majorant. This single estimate replaces Garnett's Theorem I.4.2 and is the engine of both Lemma~\ref{lem:I_5_4} and Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac}. \begin{proof} From $|e^{i\theta}-z|\ge 1-|z|$ and, by the triangle inequality and the definition of $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$, $|e^{i\theta}-z|\ge|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|-\alpha(1-|z|)$, one gets $|e^{i\theta}-z|\ge c_\alpha\bigl((1-|z|)+|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|\bigr)$; insert this into $P_z(\theta)=(1-|z|^2)/|e^{i\theta}-z|^{2}$ and use $1-|z|^2\le 2(1-|z|)$. \end{proof}

Let $
u$ be a finite positive measure carried by $\partial\D$, let $\|\zeta\|=1$, and suppose that for every $r>0$, \[ 
u(\overline B(\zeta,r)) \le c\,\sigma(\overline B(\zeta,r)). \] Then for $z\in\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$, \[ \int_{\partial\D}P_z\,d
u\le 8(\alpha+2)^2c. \]  egin{proof} Decompose the circle into dyadic chordal annuli centred at $\zeta$: with $\delta=1-|z|$, put $S_0=\overline B(\zeta,\delta)$ and $S_j=\overline B(\zeta,2^j\delta)\setminus\overline B(\zeta,2^{j-1}\delta)$. On $S_j$ the Stolz-region kernel bound gives $P_z\le 4A/(4^j\delta)$ with $A=2(\alpha+2)^2$, while the density hypothesis and the chord--arc estimate give $
u(S_j)\le c\,2^j\delta/2$; the product is $2Ac\,2^{-j}$ and $\sum_j 2^{-j}=2$, so the total is $4Ac=8(\alpha+2)^2c$, exactly the stated constant. In Lean the estimate is carried out for the lower integral, so that no piecewise integrability is needed, and transferred at the end by 	exttt{integral\_eq\_lintegral\_of\_nonneg\_ae}. Using 	exttt{lintegral\_iUnion\_le} rather than 	exttt{lintegral\_iUnion} means only that the annuli cover the plane has to be proved, not that they are pairwise disjoint. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Harmonic majorants of subharmonic functions, Garnett I.6.7
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.6.7}{Chapter I, Section 6, printed pages 36--37, PDF pages 48--49} Let $v$ be subharmonic on $\mathbb{D}$. Then $v$ has a harmonic majorant on $\mathbb{D}$ if and only if \[ \sup_{0<r<1}\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}v(r e^{i\theta})\,d\theta = \sup_{0<r<1} v_r(0) < \infty, \] where $v_r$ is the Poisson extension to $|z|<r$ of the boundary values of $v$ on $|z|=r$. When this condition holds and $v\not\equiv-\infty$, the least harmonic majorant $u$ of $v$ is given by \[ u(z)=\lim_{r\to 1} \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} P_{z/r}(\theta)v(r e^{i\theta})\,d\theta =\lim_{r\to 1}v_r(z). \] \begin{proof} The modifications $v_r$ increase and are harmonic on expanding discs. If their values at zero are bounded, Harnack's convergence theorem gives a finite harmonic limit $u\ge v$. Every harmonic majorant $U$ dominates every $v_r$ by comparison, hence dominates $u$; this proves leastness. Conversely $v_r\le U$ bounds their values at zero. The case $v\equiv-\infty$ has harmonic majorants but no least one and is excluded from the second assertion. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Garnett II.2.2: convergence and boundary size of Blaschke products
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.2.2}{Chapter II, Section 2, PDF page 64} If $m$ satisfies the Blaschke condition, then the finite partial products of $B_m$ converge uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb{D}$ to a bounded analytic function whose zeros are exactly the points with $m(w)>0$, with the prescribed multiplicities, and whose boundary modulus is one almost everywhere. More precisely, $|B_m|\le1$ on $\D$ and $\operatorname{ord}_w B_m=m(w)$ for every $w\in\D$. Its extension by zero outside $\D$ belongs to $H^\infty(\D)$. Almost everywhere on the circle, its canonical boundary value is its nontangential limit and has modulus one. \begin{proof} The passage from the product omitting origin zeros to the full product $B(z)=z^mP(z)$ is formalized: multiplication by $z^m$, whose modulus is at most one on $\D$, preserves locally uniform convergence. Analyticity of $B$ is formalized from this convergence: the finite products are holomorphic since $|\overline{a}z|<1$ for $a,z\in\D$, and a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic. The bound $|B|\le1$ is formalized by bounding each finite product and passing to the pointwise limit. The factor bound follows from $|1-\overline a z|^2-|z-a|^2=(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)\ge0$. Membership in $H^\infty$ follows from analyticity and $|B|\le1$, and the zero set is read off from the multiplicity formula, since an analytic function vanishes exactly where its order is nonzero. Convergence of the product omitting origin zeros, the multiplicity formula, and the boundary modulus remain to be proved. For the boundary modulus, first remove the origin zeros and let $B_n$ be the finite partial products. The tail product $Q_n=B/B_n$ is bounded analytic. Corollary~\ref{cor:II_3_2(p=∞)} gives \[ |Q_n(0)|\le\int_{\partial\D}|Q_n^*|\,d\sigma =\int_{\partial\D}|B^*|\,d\sigma\le1. \] Here $|B_n|=1$ on the circle and $|Q_n(0)|\to1$, so $|B^*|=1$ almost everywhere. Restoring the origin factor preserves the boundary modulus. \end{proof}

nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.2.4}{Chapter II, Section 2, PDF page 66} Let $f$ be analytic on $\mathbb D$ with $|f|\le1$. At the origin the kernel is one, giving the displayed inequality. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Outer uniqueness
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.4, outer uniqueness}{Printed page 64, PDF page 76} If two outer functions $F_1,F_2$ satisfy $|F_1^*|=|F_2^*|$ almost everywhere on $\partial\D$, then $F_1=cF_2$ on $\D$ for a constant $|c|=1$. \begin{proof} Write $F_j=C_jO_{k_j}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:outer_boundary_modulus}, $e^{k_1}=|F_1^*|=|F_2^*|=e^{k_2}$ almost everywhere, so $k_1=k_2$ almost everywhere and $\log|F_1|=P[k_1\,d\sigma]=\log|F_2|$ on $\D$. The quotient $F_1/F_2$ is analytic with modulus one, hence a unimodular constant by the maximum modulus principle. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Nevanlinna class
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.1)}{Chapter II, Section 5, printed page 66, PDF page 78} The Nevanlinna class $N$ consists of analytic functions $f$ on $\D$ such that \[ \sup_{0<r<1}\int_{\partial\D}\log^+|f(r\zeta)|\,d\sigma(\zeta)<\infty, \] where $\sigma$ is normalized arclength. In Lean, functions are extended by zero outside $\D$. \emph{Equivalent definition (Garnett (5.1)).} An analytic function $f$ belongs to $N$ if and only if $\log^+|f|$ has a harmonic majorant on $\D$. \begin{proof} For the equivalence, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} to the subharmonic function $\log^+|f|=\max(\log|f|,0)$. Conversely, a harmonic majorant $U\ge\log^+|f|\ge0$ bounds every radial $\log^+$ mean by $U(0)$, by the mean-value property. These dependencies concern the equivalence; the radial-integral definition itself needs neither result. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.2: remove the zeros of a Nevanlinna function
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.2}{Chapter II, Section 5, PDF page 78} Let $f\in N$ be nonzero and let $B$ be the Blaschke product formed from the zeros of $f$, counted with multiplicity. Then $B$ converges and $f=Bg$, where the quotient $g=f/B$, with its removable singularities filled in, is analytic and zero-free on $\mathbb{D}$, and $g$ still belongs to the Nevanlinna class. Moreover, $\log|g|$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$ on $\mathbb{D}$. \begin{proof} By (5.1), $\log|f|\le\log^+|f|\le U$ for a harmonic $U$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_1} gives the Blaschke condition, and Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} gives the least harmonic majorant $u\le U$ of $\log|f|$. Since $B$ has the zeros of $f$ with the same multiplicities (Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_2}), $f/B$ has only removable singularities; removing them gives a zero-free analytic $g$ with $f=Bg$. As $|B|\le1$, $\log|g|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$, so $u\le\log|g|$. Conversely, $u-\log|g|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log|B|$, whose least harmonic majorant is $0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_4}; hence $u=\log|g|$. Finally $\log^+|g|=\max(u,0)\le U$, so $g\in N$ by (5.1). \end{proof}

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.3: boundary values and the least-majorant measure
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.3}{Chapter II, Section 5, PDF page 79} Let $f\in N$, $f\not\equiv0$. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item $f$ has a nontangential limit $f^*(\zeta)$ at almost every $\zeta\in\partial\D$, and $f^*\ne0$ almost everywhere; \item $\log|f^*|\in L^1(d\theta/2\pi)$; \item the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$ is $P[\mu]$ for a finite signed measure $\mu$ on $\partial\D$, unique by Theorem~\ref{thm:poisson_measure_unique}, and \begin{equation} d\mu=\log|f^*|\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}+d\mu_s, \qquad \mu_s\perp d\theta . \end{equation} \end{enumerate} In other words, the absolutely continuous part of the representing measure is exactly the boundary logarithm, and the whole obstruction to the inequality $\log|f(z)|\le\int\log|f^*|P_z\,d\theta/2\pi$ is concentrated in the singular part; Garnett's class $N^+$ is the subclass where $\mu_s\le0$. \begin{proof} Let $B$ be the Blaschke product over the zeros of $f$ and $g=f/B$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:II_5_1} and Lemma~\ref{lem:II_5_2}, $g$ is zero-free and $\log|g|=P[\mu]$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:poisson_measure_unique} the measure $\mu$ is unique. Write $d\mu=k\,d\theta/2\pi+d\mu_s$ using mathlib's Lebesgue decomposition for signed measures. By Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3}, $\log|g|$ has nontangential limit $k$ almost everywhere, and since $|B^*|=1$ almost everywhere (Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_2}) the same holds for $\log|f|$. So $k\in L^1$ and \eqref{eq:II_5_3_decomposition} follow once $f$ itself is known to have nontangential limits. For that, decompose $\log|g|=u_1-u_2$ with $u_j=P[\mu_j]\ge0$ harmonic, $\mu=\mu_1-\mu_2$ the Jordan decomposition. Choose harmonic conjugates $v_j$ with $v_j(0)=0$, which exist because the disc is simply connected and which mathlib provides as \texttt{InnerProductSpace.HarmonicOnNhd.exists\_analyticOnNhd\_ball\_re\_eq}; then $\log g=(u_1+iv_1)-(u_2+iv_2)+ic$ for a real constant $c$, so that \[ g=e^{ic}\,\frac{e^{-(u_2+iv_2)}}{e^{-(u_1+iv_1)}} . \] Each $e^{-(u_j+iv_j)}$ has modulus $e^{-u_j}\le1$, hence lies in $H^\infty$ and has nontangential limits almost everywhere by Corollary~\ref{cor:II_3_1(p=∞)}. Each exponential is nonzero on the disc, so II.4.2 makes its boundary limit nonzero almost everywhere. In particular the denominator has a nonzero boundary limit, and the displayed quotient gives the finite boundary limits of $g$, and then of $f=Bg$. Combining those limits with the finite limit of $\log|g|$ identifies $k=\log|f^*|$ and proves (5.2) and (5.3). \end{proof}

nodes.name: Singular function formula
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.8)}{Printed page 70, PDF page 82} For a finite positive measure $\mu$ carried by $\partial\D$ and singular to normalized arclength $\sigma$, put \[ S_\mu(z)=\exp\left(-\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}} \frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\,d\mu(\zeta)\right). \] A function $S$ is singular on $\D$ if $S=S_\mu$ on $\D$ for some such $\mu$.

nodes.name: Garnett II, (5.9): modulus of $S_\mu$
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.9)}{Printed page 70, PDF page 82} For a finite positive measure $\mu$ carried by $\partial\D$, $S_\mu$ is analytic and zero-free on $\D$, \[ \log|S_\mu(z)|=-P[\mu](z)\quad(z\in\D), \] and $S_\mu(0)=e^{-\mu(\partial\D)}$. In particular $|S_\mu|\le1$ on $\D$. Every singular function is therefore analytic, zero-free and bounded by one on $\D$, has positive value at zero, and belongs to $H^\infty$ after extension by zero. \begin{proof} The Herglotz--Riesz transform of $\mu$ is analytic on $\D$, and its real part is $P[\mu]$ because the real part of the Herglotz--Riesz kernel is the Poisson kernel. At $z=0$ the kernel equals $1$ on $\partial\D$. Positivity of the Poisson kernel gives $P[\mu]\ge0$, hence $|S_\mu|\le1$. The representation defining a singular function transfers these properties to $S$; bounded analyticity gives membership in $H^\infty$. No boundary-limit theorem or converse characterization is used in these consequences. \end{proof}

nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.5}{Printed page 70, PDF page 82} A function $S$ is singular if and only if it is analytic on $\D$, has no zeros there, satisfies $|S|\le1$, has nontangential limits of modulus one $\sigma$-almost everywhere, and $S(0)$ is positive real. Its zero boundary limit makes the absolutely continuous part of $\mu$ vanish. Then $S/S_\mu$ is a unimodular constant, equal to one by positivity at the origin. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Algebraic structure of $N$
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.5}{Chapter II, Section 5, printed page 66, PDF page 78} $N$ is closed under sums, scalar multiples, and products. If $f\in N$ has no zeros in $\D$, then $1/f\in N$; hence $f/g\in N$ whenever $f,g\in N$ and $g$ has no zeros in $\D$. Moreover $H^p\subseteq N$ for every $p>0$. \begin{proof} Sums, scalar multiples, and products follow from $\log^+|ab|\le\log^+|a|+\log^+|b|$ and $\log^+|a+b|\le\log^+|a|+\log^+|b|+\log2$. If $U$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|f|$ and $f$ has no zeros, then $U-\log|f|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|1/f|=\log^+|f|-\log|f|$, so $1/f\in N$ by (5.1). Finally $H^p\subseteq N$ because $\log^+x\le x^p/p$. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Canonical factorization
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.10)}{Printed page 71, PDF page 83} Let $|C|=1$, let $F$ be outer, and let $\mu_1,\mu_2$ be finite positive measures carried by $\partial\D$, each singular to normalized arclength, with $\mu_1\perp\mu_2$. Then $(C,F,\mu_1,\mu_2)$ is a canonical factorization of $f$ if the zeros of $f$ in $\D$, counted with multiplicity, satisfy the Blaschke condition and, with $B$ their Blaschke product, \[ f = C\,B\,F\,S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}\quad\text{on }\D. \]

nodes.statement_short: $(C,F,\mu_1,\mu_2)$ with $f=CBFS_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}$, $B$ the Blaschke product of the zeros.
nodes.label: def:canonical_factorization

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.5: existence of canonical factorization in $N$
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.5 (existence)}{Chapter II, Section 5, PDF page 83} If $f\in N$ and $f\not\equiv0$, then $f$ has a canonical factorization $f=C\,B\,F\,S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}$ on $\D$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization
assumptions: $f\in N$ and $f\not\equiv0$
conclusions: $f$ has a canonical factorization $f=C\,B\,F\,S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}$ on $\D$
nodes.label: thm:nevanlinna_canonical_factorization

nodes.name: proof
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:II_5_2}, $f=Bg$ with $g\in N$ zero-free and $\log|g|$ the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$. By (5.2) and (5.3), that majorant is $P[k\,d\sigma+\mu_s]$ with $k=\log|f^*|\in L^1(\sigma)$ and $\mu_s\perp\sigma$; least harmonic majorants are unique, so $\log|g|=P[k\,d\sigma+\mu_s]$ on $\D$. Put $\mu_2=\mu_s^+$ and $\mu_1=\mu_s^-$, which are carried by $\partial\D$, singular to $\sigma$, and mutually singular. By linearity of the Poisson integral and (5.9), $\log|g|=\log|O_k S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}|$ on $\D$. Garnett concludes by taking a single-valued logarithm of the zero-free quotient $g$. We instead note that $g/(O_k S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2})$ is analytic on $\D$ with modulus one, hence a unimodular constant $C$ by the maximum modulus principle. This is equivalent and avoids holomorphic logarithms on the disc.

nodes.statement_short: Divide by the Blaschke product, split the representing measure into a.c. and singular parts, and match moduli; maximum modulus gives the constant.

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.5: converse
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.5 (converse)}{Printed page 71, PDF page 83} If $B$ is the Blaschke product of a multiplicity satisfying the Blaschke condition, $F$ is outer, $S_1,S_2$ are singular, and $C\in\mathbb C$, then $CBFS_1/S_2\in N$. The implemented algebraic proof permits arbitrary $C$; the book assumes $|C|=1$. \begin{proof} The convergence, analyticity and boundedness parts of II.2.2 give $B\in H^\infty\subseteq N$. Its multiplicity and boundary-modulus assertions are not used here. The elementary consequences of (5.9) give $S_1,S_2\in H^\infty\subseteq N$ and $S_2\ne0$ on $\D$, without using the full singular-function characterization. Also $F\in N$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:outer_mem_nevanlinna}. Closure of $N$ under reciprocals of zero-free functions gives $1/S_2\in N$. Multiplication and scalar multiplication then give $CBFS_1/S_2\in N$. In Lean each factor is extended by zero outside $\D$; the indicator of the product and quotient equals the corresponding product of indicators. This is the existing Lean proof. It differs from Garnett's direct signed Poisson-majorant argument: the equivalent definition in Definition~\ref{def:Nevanlinna_class} is used upstream for outer membership and reciprocal closure, but Theorem~\ref{thm:II_5_1} and its signed-measure representation are not invoked. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Harnack convergence gives $u\ge v$
nodes.statement: If their values at zero are bounded, Harnack's convergence theorem gives a finite harmonic limit $u\ge v$.
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants

nodes.name: Leastness by comparison
nodes.statement: Every harmonic majorant $U$ dominates every $v_r$ by comparison, hence dominates $u$; this proves leastness.
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely $v_r\le U$ bounds their values at zero.
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants

nodes.name: Excluded degenerate case
nodes.statement: The case $v\equiv-\infty$ has harmonic majorants but no least one and is excluded from the second assertion.
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants

nodes.name: Jensen bounds logarithmic zero sums
nodes.statement: Jensen's formula and the harmonic mean-value property bound the logarithmic zero sums.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Limit and $1-|a|\le-\log|a|$; general case via I.6.7
nodes.statement: Let the radius tend to one and use $1-|a|\le-\log|a|$ to obtain the quantitative bound. For the general case, remove the finite-order zero at the origin, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} to obtain a least harmonic majorant, and then restore the origin zero.
nodes.statement_short: Limit and $1-|a|\le-\log|a|$; general case via I.6.7
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Restoring $z^m$ preserves convergence
nodes.statement: The passage from the product omitting origin zeros to the full product $B(z)=z^mP(z)$ is formalized: multiplication by $z^m$, whose modulus is at most one on $\D$, preserves locally uniform convergence.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Analyticity of the limit
nodes.statement: Analyticity of $B$ is formalized from this convergence: the finite products are holomorphic since $|\overline{a}z|<1$ for $a,z\in\D$, and a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Bound $|B|\le1$
nodes.statement: The bound $|B|\le1$ is formalized by bounding each finite product and passing to the pointwise limit.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Factor bound identity
nodes.statement: The factor bound follows from $|1-\overline a z|^2-|z-a|^2=(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)\ge0$.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: $H^\infty$ membership and zero set
nodes.statement: Membership in $H^\infty$ follows from analyticity and $|B|\le1$, and the zero set is read off from the multiplicity formula, since an analytic function vanishes exactly where its order is nonzero.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Open parts
nodes.statement: Convergence of the product omitting origin zeros, the multiplicity formula, and the boundary modulus remain to be proved.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Tail products $Q_n$
nodes.statement: For the boundary modulus, first remove the origin zeros and let $B_n$ be the finite partial products. The tail product $Q_n=B/B_n$ is bounded analytic.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Bound $|Q_n(0)|$ by boundary integral
nodes.statement: Corollary~\ref{cor:II_3_2(p=∞)} gives \[ |Q_n(0)|\le\int_{\partial\D}|Q_n^*|\,d\sigma =\int_{\partial\D}|B^*|\,d\sigma\le1. \]
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Conclude $|B^*|=1$ a.e.
nodes.statement: Here $|B_n|=1$ on the circle and $|Q_n(0)|\to1$, so $|B^*|=1$ almost everywhere. Restoring the origin factor preserves the boundary modulus.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: (a)$\Rightarrow$(b)
nodes.statement: For $(a)\Rightarrow(b)$, remove a finite initial Blaschke product so that the remaining product has modulus at the origin arbitrarily close to one; apply the subharmonic mean inequality and let the radius tend to one.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: (b)$\Leftrightarrow$(c) via I.6.7 and maximum principle
nodes.statement: For $(b)\Leftrightarrow(c)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} identifies the radial limit with $u(0)$ for the least harmonic majorant $u\le0$. The harmonic maximum principle gives $u(0)=0$ if and only if $u\equiv0$. This equivalence is formalized using the existing prerequisite theorems; the proof of $(a)\Rightarrow(b)$ remains to be formalized.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products

nodes.name: Parts are Poisson integrals by I.3.5(a)
nodes.statement: The real and imaginary parts of $f$ are bounded harmonic, hence Poisson integrals of $L^\infty$ boundary data by Theorem~\ref{thm:I_3_5(a)} with $p=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Parts are Poisson integrals by I.3.5(a)
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: Fatou at Lebesgue points
nodes.statement: These densities lie in $L^1$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac} gives their nontangential limits almost everywhere.
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: Combine real and imaginary limits
nodes.statement: Intersect the two full-measure sets and combine the real and imaginary limits.
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: $H^\infty$ case and status
nodes.statement: The $H^\infty$ case uses the equality of the Hardy norm with the pointwise supremum. Both Lean proofs are complete; I.3.5(a) remains an unproved prerequisite.
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: Represent the parts via I.3.5(a)
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_3_5(a)} to the real and imaginary parts of a bounded analytic function.
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: Identify densities with boundary values
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac} identifies the resulting densities with its boundary values.
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, positivity and unit mass of the Poisson kernel give the $L^\infty$ bound, and Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac} gives the prescribed boundary values.
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: Displayed inequality at the origin
nodes.statement: At the origin the kernel is one, giving the displayed inequality.
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values

nodes.name: Apply I.6.7 with dominated convergence and Fatou
nodes.statement: Follow Garnett's proof: apply I.6.7 to $\log|f|$, use dominated convergence for the positive logarithmic parts and Fatou's lemma for the negative parts, then remove a possible zero at the origin.
nodes.statement_short: Apply I.6.7 with dominated convergence and Fatou
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Constant dominates positive parts
nodes.statement: In the bounded case a constant dominates the positive parts.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Scope note
nodes.statement: This is the case used below; the full $0<p<\infty$ theorem additionally uses the integrable maximal function of II.3.1 and is not asserted here.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: II.4.1 makes the boundary logarithm integrable
nodes.statement: For nonzero $f$, II.4.1 makes the extended boundary logarithm integrable, whereas it is $-\infty$ wherever $f^*=0$.
nodes.statement_short: II.4.1 makes the boundary logarithm integrable
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Zero set is null
nodes.statement: Thus that set has measure zero.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Order of dependencies
nodes.statement: This result precedes and is used by II.5.3; it is not derived from it.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Herglotz integral analytic with real part $P[k\,d\sigma]$
nodes.statement: The integral $\int\frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\,k(\zeta)\,d\sigma(\zeta)$ is analytic in $z\in\D$, and its real part is $P[k\,d\sigma](z)$ because the real part of the Herglotz--Riesz kernel is the Poisson kernel.
nodes.statement_short: Herglotz integral analytic with real part $P[k\,d\sigma]$
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Exponentiate and multiply by $C$
nodes.statement: Exponentiating gives the claims for $O_k$; multiplying by $|C|=1$ gives those for $F$.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: No boundary theorem used
nodes.statement: No Nevanlinna boundary theorem is used here.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Necessity by II.4.1
nodes.statement: Necessity is II.4.1.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Construct $\exp(u+iv)$
nodes.statement: For sufficiency use Garnett's construction $\exp(u+iv)$, where $u=P[\log h\,d\sigma]$ and $v$ is its normalized harmonic conjugate.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Boundedness
nodes.statement: The bound $u\le\log\|h\|_\infty$ gives boundedness.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Boundary moduli equal $h$
nodes.statement: Bounded-analytic Fatou gives complex boundary limits, and Poisson Fatou identifies their moduli with $h$.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Scope note
nodes.statement: The finite-$p$ refinement in the book is not needed for the factorization roadmap.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Arbitrary integrable data allowed
nodes.statement: The book's outer construction permits arbitrary integrable logarithmic data.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Write $O_k=O_{-k^-}/O_{-k^+}$
nodes.statement: To justify finite complex boundary limits without II.5.3, write $k=k^+-k^-$ and $O_k=O_{-k^-}/O_{-k^+}$.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Apply II.4.4 to both factors
nodes.statement: Apply the bounded construction II.4.4 to $e^{-k^-}$ and $e^{-k^+}$; their boundary moduli are positive almost everywhere.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Quotient has modulus $e^k$
nodes.statement: Taking the quotient gives modulus $e^k$.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Role of the argument
nodes.statement: This supplies the disc-form detail behind the boundary assertion after the outer definition, independently of Nevanlinna boundary theory.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Boundary moduli give $k_1=k_2$ a.e.
nodes.statement: Write $F_j=C_jO_{k_j}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:outer_boundary_modulus}, $e^{k_1}=|F_1^*|=|F_2^*|=e^{k_2}$ almost everywhere, so $k_1=k_2$ almost everywhere and $\log|F_1|=P[k_1\,d\sigma]=\log|F_2|$ on $\D$.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Maximum modulus principle
nodes.statement: The quotient $F_1/F_2$ is analytic with modulus one, hence a unimodular constant by the maximum modulus principle.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions

nodes.name: Apply I.6.7 to $\log^+|f|$
nodes.statement: For the equivalence, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} to the subharmonic function $\log^+|f|=\max(\log|f|,0)$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Converse via mean-value property
nodes.statement: Conversely, a harmonic majorant $U\ge\log^+|f|\ge0$ bounds every radial $\log^+$ mean by $U(0)$, by the mean-value property.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Scope of dependencies
nodes.statement: These dependencies concern the equivalence; the radial-integral definition itself needs neither result.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Choose majorants $U$ and least majorant $u$
nodes.statement: If $f\in N$, take a nonnegative harmonic majorant $U$ of $\log^+|f|$ and let $u\le U$ be the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$, which exists since $f\not\equiv0$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Represent and subtract measures
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_3_5(c)} to $U$ and $U-u$ and subtract their representing measures to obtain $u=P[\mu]$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Converse via $P[\mu^+]$ majorant
nodes.statement: Conversely, the Jordan identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson_integral_linear}) gives, even if $P[\mu]$ is only a majorant rather than the least one, $\log^+|f|\le P[\mu^+]$, a nonnegative harmonic majorant; hence $f\in N$ by the equivalent definition in Definition~\ref{def:Nevanlinna_class}.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Blaschke condition and least majorant $u$
nodes.statement: By (5.1), $\log|f|\le\log^+|f|\le U$ for a harmonic $U$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_1} gives the Blaschke condition, and Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} gives the least harmonic majorant $u\le U$ of $\log|f|$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Construct zero-free $g=f/B$
nodes.statement: Since $B$ has the zeros of $f$ with the same multiplicities (Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_2}), $f/B$ has only removable singularities; removing them gives a zero-free analytic $g$ with $f=Bg$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: $u\le\log|g|$
nodes.statement: As $|B|\le1$, $\log|g|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$, so $u\le\log|g|$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: $u=\log|g|$ via II.2.4
nodes.statement: Conversely, $u-\log|g|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log|B|$, whose least harmonic majorant is $0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_4}; hence $u=\log|g|$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: $g\in N$
nodes.statement: Finally $\log^+|g|=\max(u,0)\le U$, so $g\in N$ by (5.1).
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Introduce $B$ and $g$
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the Blaschke product over the zeros of $f$ and $g=f/B$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:II_5_1} and Lemma~\ref{lem:II_5_2}, $g$ is zero-free and $\log|g|=P[\mu]$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:poisson_measure_unique} the measure $\mu$ is unique.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Lebesgue decomposition
nodes.statement: Write $d\mu=k\,d\theta/2\pi+d\mu_s$ using mathlib's Lebesgue decomposition for signed measures.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Fatou gives limit $k$
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3}, $\log|g|$ has nontangential limit $k$ almost everywhere, and since $|B^*|=1$ almost everywhere (Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_2}) the same holds for $\log|f|$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Reduce to existence of limits of $f$
nodes.statement: So $k\in L^1$ and \eqref{eq:II_5_3_decomposition} follow once $f$ itself is known to have nontangential limits.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to existence of limits of $f$
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Jordan-split $\log|g|$
nodes.statement: For that, decompose $\log|g|=u_1-u_2$ with $u_j=P[\mu_j]\ge0$ harmonic, $\mu=\mu_1-\mu_2$ the Jordan decomposition.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Write $g$ as a quotient of exponentials
nodes.statement: Choose harmonic conjugates $v_j$ with $v_j(0)=0$, which exist because the disc is simply connected and which mathlib provides as \texttt{InnerProductSpace.HarmonicOnNhd.exists\_analyticOnNhd\_ball\_re\_eq}; then $\log g=(u_1+iv_1)-(u_2+iv_2)+ic$ for a real constant $c$, so that \[ g=e^{ic}\,\frac{e^{-(u_2+iv_2)}}{e^{-(u_1+iv_1)}} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $g$ as a quotient of exponentials
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Bounded factors have limits by II.3.1
nodes.statement: Each $e^{-(u_j+iv_j)}$ has modulus $e^{-u_j}\le1$, hence lies in $H^\infty$ and has nontangential limits almost everywhere by Corollary~\ref{cor:II_3_1(p=∞)}.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded factors have limits by II.3.1
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: II.4.2 makes limits nonzero
nodes.statement: Each exponential is nonzero on the disc, so II.4.2 makes its boundary limit nonzero almost everywhere.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Boundary limits of $g$ and $f$
nodes.statement: In particular the denominator has a nonzero boundary limit, and the displayed quotient gives the finite boundary limits of $g$, and then of $f=Bg$.
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Identify $k=\log|f^*|$
nodes.statement: Combining those limits with the finite limit of $\log|g|$ identifies $k=\log|f^*|$ and proves (5.2) and (5.3).
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures

nodes.name: Real part is $P[\mu]$
nodes.statement: The Herglotz--Riesz transform of $\mu$ is analytic on $\D$, and its real part is $P[\mu]$ because the real part of the Herglotz--Riesz kernel is the Poisson kernel.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: Value at origin
nodes.statement: At $z=0$ the kernel equals $1$ on $\partial\D$.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: $|S_\mu|\le1$
nodes.statement: Positivity of the Poisson kernel gives $P[\mu]\ge0$, hence $|S_\mu|\le1$.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: Transfer to singular functions
nodes.statement: The representation defining a singular function transfers these properties to $S$; bounded analyticity gives membership in $H^\infty$.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: No boundary theorem used
nodes.statement: No boundary-limit theorem or converse characterization is used in these consequences.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: Analyticity and modulus formula
nodes.statement: The exponential integral is analytic and satisfies $\log|S_\mu|=-P[\mu]$.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: Forward properties via I.5.4 and Fatou
nodes.statement: Positivity, the singular Poisson boundary theorem, and bounded-analytic Fatou give the four properties.
nodes.statement_short: Forward properties via I.5.4 and Fatou
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: Represent $-\log|S|$ as $P[\mu]$
nodes.statement: Conversely, represent the nonnegative harmonic function $-\log|S|$ as $P[\mu]$.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: A.c. part vanishes
nodes.statement: Its zero boundary limit makes the absolutely continuous part of $\mu$ vanish.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: Quotient is constant one
nodes.statement: Then $S/S_\mu$ is a unimodular constant, equal to one by positivity at the origin.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors

nodes.name: Closure via $\log^+$ inequalities
nodes.statement: Sums, scalar multiples, and products follow from $\log^+|ab|\le\log^+|a|+\log^+|b|$ and $\log^+|a+b|\le\log^+|a|+\log^+|b|+\log2$.
nodes.section: 1.9 Nevanlinna closure and outer membership

nodes.name: Reciprocal closure
nodes.statement: If $U$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|f|$ and $f$ has no zeros, then $U-\log|f|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|1/f|=\log^+|f|-\log|f|$, so $1/f\in N$ by (5.1).
nodes.section: 1.9 Nevanlinna closure and outer membership

nodes.name: $H^p\subseteq N$
nodes.statement: Finally $H^p\subseteq N$ because $\log^+x\le x^p/p$.
nodes.section: 1.9 Nevanlinna closure and outer membership

nodes.name: Remove zeros
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:II_5_2}, $f=Bg$ with $g\in N$ zero-free and $\log|g|$ the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Majorant is $P[k\,d\sigma+\mu_s]$
nodes.statement: By (5.2) and (5.3), that majorant is $P[k\,d\sigma+\mu_s]$ with $k=\log|f^*|\in L^1(\sigma)$ and $\mu_s\perp\sigma$; least harmonic majorants are unique, so $\log|g|=P[k\,d\sigma+\mu_s]$ on $\D$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Singular measures from Jordan parts
nodes.statement: Put $\mu_2=\mu_s^+$ and $\mu_1=\mu_s^-$, which are carried by $\partial\D$, singular to $\sigma$, and mutually singular.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Match moduli
nodes.statement: By linearity of the Poisson integral and (5.9), $\log|g|=\log|O_k S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}|$ on $\D$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Garnett's route
nodes.statement: Garnett concludes by taking a single-valued logarithm of the zero-free quotient $g$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Maximum modulus gives unimodular $C$
nodes.statement: We instead note that $g/(O_k S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2})$ is analytic on $\D$ with modulus one, hence a unimodular constant $C$ by the maximum modulus principle.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Avoids holomorphic logarithms
nodes.statement: This is equivalent and avoids holomorphic logarithms on the disc.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Book proof
nodes.statement: Follow Garnett. The zeros of $f$ determine $B$. Since $|B^*|=|S_1^*|=|S_2^*|=1$ almost everywhere, both outer factors have boundary modulus $|f^*|$. Outer uniqueness determines $F$ up to phase; in particular $\log|F|=P[\log|f^*|\,d\sigma]$. By II.5.2, $u=\log|f/B|$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$. Formula (5.9) gives \[ u-\log|F|=P[\mu_2-\mu_1]=P[\nu_2-\nu_1]. \] Poisson uniqueness identifies the signed measures, and their mutually singular Jordan decompositions identify each positive measure. Cancel the common nonzero singular factors and cancel $B$ away from its isolated zeros, then extend by continuity, to obtain $CF=C'F'$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Zeros determine $B$
nodes.statement: Follow Garnett. The zeros of $f$ determine $B$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Outer factors have modulus $|f^*|$; outer uniqueness
nodes.statement: Since $|B^*|=|S_1^*|=|S_2^*|=1$ almost everywhere, both outer factors have boundary modulus $|f^*|$. Outer uniqueness determines $F$ up to phase; in particular $\log|F|=P[\log|f^*|\,d\sigma]$.
nodes.statement_short: Outer factors have modulus $|f^*|$; outer uniqueness
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Least majorant and (5.9)
nodes.statement: By II.5.2, $u=\log|f/B|$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$. Formula (5.9) gives \[ u-\log|F|=P[\mu_2-\mu_1]=P[\nu_2-\nu_1]. \]
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Identify measures
nodes.statement: Poisson uniqueness identifies the signed measures, and their mutually singular Jordan decompositions identify each positive measure.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Cancel to get $CF=C'F'$
nodes.statement: Cancel the common nonzero singular factors and cancel $B$ away from its isolated zeros, then extend by continuity, to obtain $CF=C'F'$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Implementation status
nodes.statement: \emph{Implementation status.} The linked Lean theorem currently has a proof using the measure representing $\log|CFS_1/S_2|$ and Lebesgue decomposition, without outer boundary uniqueness or II.5.2. That proof is preserved, but the book proof displayed here has not yet been implemented and is not marked complete.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: $B\in N$ via II.2.2
nodes.statement: The convergence, analyticity and boundedness parts of II.2.2 give $B\in H^\infty\subseteq N$. Its multiplicity and boundary-modulus assertions are not used here.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: $S_j\in N$ via (5.9); $F\in N$
nodes.statement: The elementary consequences of (5.9) give $S_1,S_2\in H^\infty\subseteq N$ and $S_2\ne0$ on $\D$, without using the full singular-function characterization. Also $F\in N$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:outer_mem_nevanlinna}.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Reciprocal closure
nodes.statement: Closure of $N$ under reciprocals of zero-free functions gives $1/S_2\in N$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Product in $N$
nodes.statement: Multiplication and scalar multiplication then give $CBFS_1/S_2\in N$.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Lean extension by zero
nodes.statement: In Lean each factor is extended by zero outside $\D$; the indicator of the product and quotient equals the corresponding product of indicators.
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization

nodes.name: Comparison with Garnett
